title: The Delivery

jokes.text: Pam announces her pregnancy to a client as a sales tactic during her maternity leave check-in call
jokes.setup: Pam is calling clients before maternity leave to check if they need anything — a professional, considerate gesture
jokes.punchline: She immediately exploits the pregnancy for a sale, undermining the goodwill framing
jokes.explanation: Solid cold open joke that quickly establishes the sales-office world. The irony of Pam doing the exact thing Jim objects to is funny but not exceptional — it's a well-worn 'pot calls kettle black' structure.

jokes.text: Jim announces the pregnancy to a client on a sales call: 'Hey, did I tell you we're gonna have a baby?'
jokes.setup: Jim just criticized Pam for exploiting the pregnancy for sales
jokes.punchline: He immediately does the exact same thing on his next call
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured immediate callback. The setup and payoff happen within seconds of each other, making the hypocrisy land perfectly. Jim's self-aware smirk (implied by the 'Oh.' that follows) elevates it. The economy is excellent — one line does all the work.

jokes.text: Dwight's client says he could use the paper money because his cousin got a 'nasty new goat fungus' that 'bearded so quickly'
jokes.setup: Dwight is making a sales call, trying to compete with Jim and Pam's pregnancy advantage
jokes.punchline: The client's cousin has a specific, horrific, vivid fungal condition involving goats and bearding
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'goat fungus' and 'beard so quickly' is genuinely funny and weird. It's a glimpse into Dwight's world where even his clients are strange. Slightly undercut by being in a phone call we only hear one side of.

jokes.text: Dwight in talking head: 'I need a baby. I'll never outsell Jim and Pam without one.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been watching Jim and Pam exploit the pregnancy for sales
jokes.punchline: Dwight's solution is simply to acquire a baby — treated as a business problem with an obvious business solution
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight logic — utterly cold and transactional framing of something deeply human. 'I need a baby' as a competitive business strategy is pitch-perfect character comedy. The delivery would be completely deadpan, which is exactly right. High character integration score because only Dwight arrives at this conclusion.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head continuation: 'Also, I've been noticing a gaping hole in my life.'
jokes.setup: Dwight just said he needs a baby for business reasons, implying pure pragmatism
jokes.punchline: The beat reveals he also has a genuine emotional need — but delivered with the same flat affect, making it funnier and sadder simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The pause between the business reason and the emotional admission is perfectly timed. It's a rare moment of Dwight vulnerability filtered through his robotic delivery, making it both funny and unexpectedly touching. Two beats in one confessional that escalate beautifully.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'Sometimes I wake up cradling a gourd.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has admitted to a gaping hole in his life and a subconscious desire for a child
jokes.punchline: His unconscious parenting instinct manifests as cradling a gourd — the most Dwight-ian possible substitute for a baby
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. A three-beat confessional that escalates from cold business logic → vulnerability → absurdist image. 'Cradling a gourd' is five words of perfect television comedy. The gourd is Dwight's farm, Schrute Beet Farms, his self-sufficiency, his weirdness — all in one specific object. It's quotable, character-specific, original, and lands with genuine comedic force. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor; arguably exceeds it in character integration.

jokes.text: Kevin describes cooking through The Twilight Cookbook: 'Last night I had Edward's cornflake chicken.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is being praised as a gourmand for cooking through Julia Child's cookbook
jokes.punchline: He's also halfway through The Twilight Cookbook, treating vampire teen fiction tie-in merchandise as serious culinary literature
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of high culinary culture (Julia Child) with Twilight tie-in merch is a great Kevin joke. Specific enough to be funny — 'Edward's cornflake chicken' has exactly the right specificity. Slightly dated by the Twilight reference but was very timely for 2010.

jokes.text: Kevin's eating schedule with Pam: 'Second breakfast, lunch, second lunch and first dinner.'
jokes.setup: Kevin says he and pregnant Pam have been eating together a lot because they get hungry at the same times
jokes.punchline: His 'a lot' means four meals per day with escalating Hobbit-style naming conventions
jokes.explanation: The list structure is perfect — 'second breakfast' is already funny, then 'second lunch' and 'first dinner' escalate the joke by implying there will be more dinners. The qualifier 'not all meals, just...' before the absurd list is a great setup. High character integration because Kevin's food obsession is central to his character.

jokes.text: Kevin proposes 'one last ultra feast' before Pam goes to the hospital
jokes.setup: Pam is in early labor and Kevin wants to do something special
jokes.punchline: His version of 'something special' is a ceremonial feast he has named and treated with ritualistic gravitas
jokes.explanation: The coinage of 'ultra feast' as a named event with its own solemnity is a good Kevin joke — it's the absurdity of treating gluttony as ceremony. Gets paid off later in the episode.

jokes.text: Jim explains the insurance midnight scheme, then adds: 'once we bring the baby home, if it's crying all night, one of us is gonna have to take care of it, and I do not plan on helping unless it's a boy.'
jokes.setup: Jim is explaining the rational reasons for waiting until midnight to go to the hospital
jokes.punchline: He undercuts the responsible framing by admitting he'll only help with the baby if it's a boy — a joke Pam immediately flags as tired
jokes.explanation: Functional joke. The meta-commentary from Pam ('I cannot wait for that joke to be over') is actually funnier than the joke itself — the writers know it's a thin bit and have Pam call it out, which partially redeems it.

jokes.text: Pam: 'I cannot wait for that joke to be over.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been making his 'only helping if it's a boy' joke repeatedly throughout the pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Pam breaks the fourth wall slightly by commenting on the joke itself as a joke she's tired of
jokes.explanation: This is the better joke in the pair. Pam treating Jim's recurring bit as a piece of comedy she's endured is relatable and meta without being too clever. The weariness is perfectly in character for a woman in labor listening to her husband riff.

jokes.text: Michael announces he put diesel in Jim's car 'to save some money' and then 'did a heck of a job baby-proofing this office'
jokes.setup: Michael wants to be helpful to Jim and Pam before the birth
jokes.punchline: His 'help' includes sabotaging the car with the wrong fuel and baby-proofing a place the baby will never live
jokes.explanation: Two-part Michael stupidity joke that escalates nicely. The diesel fuel is a practical disaster; the baby-proofing reveal adds a layer of delusional thinking. Both are character-perfect for Michael.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Also, I did a heck of a job baby-proofing this office.' Jim: 'You know the baby's not gonna live here, right?'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to be helpful with the baby.
jokes.punchline: Michael has baby-proofed the workplace — a task that didn't need doing — because he apparently believes the baby will reside there.
jokes.explanation: Michael's total failure to understand how babies work is well-mined here. The implicit visual joke of an office with baby-proofing is funny. Jim's deadpan correction is pitch-perfect straight-man work.

jokes.text: 'Well, the baby was conceived here, so might as well live here a little bit, too.' / 'That logic's airtight, but unfortunately it wasn't conceived here.' / [beat] / 'Burning Man, Porta Potty.'
jokes.setup: Michael argues the baby should live at the office since it was conceived there
jokes.punchline: Jim agrees the logic is airtight but corrects the factual premise — then Pam reveals the actual conception location: a Burning Man Porta Potty
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure that's nearly perfectly constructed. Jim's 'That logic's airtight, but...' is a great straight-man move, and 'Burning Man, Porta Potty' lands as a shocking, specific, disgusting punchline that recontextualizes the Halperts. Michael's 'Yuck! TMI. How was it?' is a bonus laugh — he immediately asks for details despite just saying TMI. One of the episode's best crafted jokes.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Yuck! TMI. How was it?' — immediately after Pam says the baby was conceived in a Burning Man Porta Potty
jokes.setup: Michael expresses disgust at the Porta Potty revelation
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks for more details, contradicting his own 'TMI' reaction
jokes.explanation: Perfect Michael character beat. He performs propriety ('TMI') but can't resist prurience ('How was it?') — this is exactly who Michael Scott is. The line is short, funny, and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Yuck! TMI. How was it?'
jokes.setup: Pam has just revealed the baby was conceived in a Burning Man Porta Potty
jokes.punchline: Michael declares 'TMI' — then immediately asks for more information about it
jokes.explanation: The contradiction of 'TMI' followed immediately by 'How was it?' is a perfect Michael Scott behavior — his voyeurism overrides his professed propriety. Tight, character-specific, and a great button on the Burning Man reveal.

jokes.text: Random office worker Nick warns Pam: 'You don't want to wait too long, otherwise the baby's gonna become a teenager in there, and you'll be up all night from the rock music.'
jokes.setup: The office is weighing in on Pam's decision to wait until midnight
jokes.punchline: A background character offers biologically impossible but internally logical advice about in-utero adolescence
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist joke from a peripheral character. The logic of the teenager-in-the-womb is committed and specific enough to work. Michael's immediate 'Shut up, Nick. God! What a weird thing to say' is the right reaction.

jokes.text: Michael stares Nick down: 'Weird IT nerd. Don't get revenge on me, nerd.' Then continues staring: 'What are you looking at? Nerd.'
jokes.setup: Michael reprimands Nick for saying a weird thing
jokes.punchline: Michael's response is to bully Nick in the most childish possible way — calling him a nerd repeatedly while escalating the confrontation he started
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael overreaction — he escalates a minor moment into a standoff with someone he has power over. 'Don't get revenge on me, nerd' is a specific kind of Michael paranoia (fear of IT revenge) that's character-rich.

jokes.text: Dwight to Angela: 'Bear my child.' / Long pause / 'Excuse me?' / 'I want to have a child for business reasons and I want you to be the mother. If you agree, say nothing. If you disagree, say anything.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants to proposition Angela
jokes.punchline: He frames it as a business proposition with an absurd consent mechanism — silence means yes
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'If you agree, say nothing. If you disagree, say anything.' is a genuinely clever inversion that could only come from Dwight's desire for maximum control. It also references their complicated history. The beat before 'Excuse me?' makes this land perfectly. High across all categories — original framing, tight structure, completely character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Very well. Let's meet at 4:00 p.m. In our old meeting spot and bang it out.'
jokes.setup: Angela's silence (per Dwight's consent rule) has implied agreement
jokes.punchline: Dwight treats the conception as a scheduled meeting in a familiar location, using 'bang it out' with complete businesslike neutrality
jokes.explanation: 'Bang it out' as corporate euphemism for sex is a classic double entendre but the framing — 'our old meeting spot,' the scheduling — makes it feel fresh and specific to these characters' secretive history. The economy of the line is excellent.

jokes.text: Contractions hit seven minutes apart and Michael panics: 'Contraptions! She's contrapting!'
jokes.setup: Michael is monitoring the contractions
jokes.punchline: He mispronounces 'contractions' as 'contraptions' and turns it into a verb: 'contrapting'
jokes.explanation: Michael's malapropism is characteristically him — he confidently mispronounces in a moment of crisis. 'She's contrapting' as a verb is the bonus laugh. Classic Michael word-mangling.

jokes.text: Kevin warns Jim and Pam against waiting: if the baby is born tomorrow, she'll share a birthday with 'Buttmud Brooks, my old roommate'
jokes.setup: Kevin is warning against waiting for the insurance midnight cutoff
jokes.punchline: His reason is a person named 'Buttmud Brooks' — a name so specific and ridiculous it implies a whole backstory
jokes.explanation: 'Buttmud Brooks' is a great comedy name — specific, visceral, and totally inexplicable. The fact that Kevin had a roommate named this, treats it as relevant information, and then Jim and Pam both separately register 'Did you hear that? Buttmud Brooks' is a perfect three-way comedic beat. High quotability — 'Buttmud Brooks' becomes its own punchline that the episode references again.

jokes.text: Jim talking head about Pam calling the audible on contractions: 'That's her call, 'cause she's the quarterback. I'm just the left tackle who happened to get her pregnant.'
jokes.setup: Jim is explaining the shift from 7-minute to 5-minute contraction threshold
jokes.punchline: He uses sports metaphor to describe his role, then undercuts the metaphor by noting the left tackle's unusual role in conception
jokes.explanation: The sports metaphor works because Jim is a self-deprecating everyman who would actually frame things this way. The punchline of the left tackle 'getting her pregnant' is a good tag. Competent Jim talking-head humor.

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'Guys, a word of advice, speaking as a former baby...'
jokes.setup: Andy is about to give advice about baby names
jokes.punchline: 'Speaking as a former baby' — a credential everyone has but no one would ever cite
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's tightest jokes. The phrase 'speaking as a former baby' establishes Andy's oblivious pomposity perfectly — he presents a universal human experience as a unique credential. Maximum economy. High quotability.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: He was named Walter Junior, but when his brother was born, the parents felt the brother 'better exemplified the Walter Junior name' and gave it to him, leaving Andy with 'Andrew' from a baby name book.
jokes.setup: Andy is giving baby name advice based on his personal experience
jokes.punchline: His parents literally took his name and gave it to his younger sibling because they felt he didn't live up to it — one of the darkest things ever casually mentioned on The Office
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy because it reframes everything about Andy's overcompensating, approval-seeking personality in a single backstory beat. His parents replacing his name because he didn't 'exemplify' it is genuinely disturbing and hilarious. Andy then adds that they got 'Andrew' out of a baby name book — a completely random afterthought — which deepens the wound. One of the darkest character-building jokes in the series, delivered completely matter-of-factly. Earns its 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Michael's solution to distract Pam: 'Conference room, five minutes. No, no, five seconds! Right now, right now, conference room.' Topic announced: 'Potpourri.'
jokes.setup: Michael wants to help Pam by organizing a distraction
jokes.punchline: He calls a conference room meeting with the urgency of a crisis and announces the topic as 'Potpourri' — the most trivially meaningless subject possible
jokes.explanation: Michael's ability to treat the trivial with the urgency of an emergency is well-deployed here. 'Five minutes. No, five seconds! Right now!' is a good escalation, and 'Potpourri' as the crisis topic is a great anti-climax.

jokes.text: Michael talking head brags about always being able to distract others in class, which his teachers praised as a skill
jokes.setup: Michael describes himself as 'a master of distraction'
jokes.punchline: His evidence is that his teachers 'complimented' him for distracting other students — a clear misreading of being repeatedly reprimanded
jokes.explanation: Standard Michael self-delusion beat — he reinterprets criticism as praise. Competent and character-consistent but not the episode's sharpest version of this joke type.

jokes.text: Michael asks if anyone can try to think of the first 13 colonies as a distraction — cut to awkward silence and mumbling
jokes.setup: Michael has called a meeting to distract Pam from labor pains with... general topics
jokes.punchline: The room has no response to being asked to recite colonial history as entertainment
jokes.explanation: The awkward silence here is mild but real. The visual joke is the room genuinely trying to engage with a terrible distraction activity while Pam is in labor next to them.

jokes.text: Office member suggests 'Can we do sleight-of-hand tricks?' — Michael approves; someone immediately says 'I'm gonna go look at the Internet.'
jokes.setup: The office is trying to come up with distraction ideas
jokes.punchline: Someone's immediate exit to 'look at the Internet' rather than participate is a perfect workplace deflection
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna go look at the Internet' is a great deadpan exit line — it's the most meaningless possible reason to leave a meeting and captures 2010 office life perfectly.

jokes.text: Phyllis offers to 'put on lipstick the way Molly Ringwald does in The Breakfast Club.' Michael immediately says: 'No, no. I don't think anybody wants to see that.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks if anyone has special skills for the distraction
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's surprising special skill is rejected immediately and completely — Michael's blunt dismissal is the laugh
jokes.explanation: The Breakfast Club lipstick trick is a specific enough cultural reference to be funny coming from Phyllis. Michael's flat 'No, no. I don't think anybody wants to see that' is casually cruel in the way Michael often is without meaning to be.

jokes.text: Kevin stops his silent dance because someone is clapping — 'You're clapping. I need complete silence.' — then announces he has to start over: 'The Evolution of Dance dance.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is performing his silent dance; someone applauds
jokes.punchline: He is derailed by applause — the most supportive possible disruption — and restarts from the very beginning with full formal announcement
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Kevin's neurotic silence requirement being violated by applause is a perfect comic escalation. His re-announcement 'The Evolution of Dance dance' with full gravitas is excellent.

jokes.text: As Kevin dances in silence, Dwight recites Triple Crown winners and jockey names, and someone sings a mournful song — all simultaneously
jokes.setup: Kevin is performing his silent distraction dance; others are contributing
jokes.punchline: The 'distraction' has devolved into a chaos of racing trivia, sad folk music, and silent dancing happening simultaneously in an office where a woman is in labor
jokes.explanation: The visual chaos is the joke — a transcription can barely capture it. Dwight reciting horse racing history ('Affirmed, Seattle Slew, Secretariat...') while someone sings a dirge while Kevin dances silently is peak Office absurdism. Works better visually than on paper.

jokes.text: Dwight and Angela's parenting contract: child will be breastfed 'exactly six months' then weaned onto 'nutrient-rich, winter vegetable mash provided by the father, Dwight Schrute, hereafter referred to as Morpheus.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has drawn up a legal parenting contract before they conceive
jokes.punchline: The contract names Dwight as 'Morpheus' — a Greek god/Matrix character chosen as his parenting alias — with full legal formality
jokes.explanation: The parenting contract is a great Dwight bit, and 'hereafter referred to as Morpheus' is the best detail. It's in a legal document. He chose Morpheus. No explanation given. The specificity and commitment to the absurdity makes this exceptional character comedy. Only Dwight would name himself Morpheus in a parenting contract.

jokes.text: Kevin is calculating contractions: 'We have every six minutes, ladies and gentlemen. Another 75 contractions and you are going to be there. For the love of God, Pam, do it for ultra feast.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is monitoring Pam's progress
jokes.punchline: His encouragement to endure labor is entirely motivated by wanting to have the ultra feast — he uses math to frame Pam's suffering in terms of food delay
jokes.explanation: 'For the love of God, Pam, do it for ultra feast' is a great line — Kevin reduces Pam's labor to an obstacle between him and dinner. The math ('75 contractions') adds a nice layer of Kevin actually having done the calculation.

jokes.text: Michael has printed '10 ways to induce labor' and proposes doing the opposite to slow it down. Erin reads the first one: 'Stimulate the nipples.' Michael: 'Okay, nobody touch Pam's nipples. Think of Pam's nipples as Toby's grundle.'
jokes.setup: Michael's plan to slow labor by reversing induction methods
jokes.punchline: His instruction about not touching nipples uses Toby's 'grundle' as the most repulsive possible comparison to ensure compliance
jokes.explanation: The Toby grundle comparison is perfectly Michael — crass, HR-violating, and targeting his least favorite employee. It's a great escalation of the nipple-stimulation premise. The specific choice of 'Toby's grundle' over any other repulsive comparison is deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Erin reads: 'Her shirt is touching them. Maybe we should cut holes in her shirt.' Someone offers: 'I have a shirt like that in my car.'
jokes.setup: Michael has told the office to keep Pam's nipples unstimulated
jokes.punchline: The logical escalation is cutting holes in her shirt, which someone is immediately prepared to facilitate with a shirt they already own
jokes.explanation: The escalation of 'cut holes in the shirt' followed by someone having such a shirt immediately on hand is a nice Office absurdist moment. The mystery of why they own this shirt is funnier than any explanation.

jokes.text: Third anti-induction item: 'Eat spicy foods.' Michael interprets 'opposite' as: 'Stick spicy food up her butt.'
jokes.setup: Michael is doing the opposite of induction methods — opposite of 'eat spicy foods'
jokes.punchline: Michael's interpretation of 'opposite of eating' is insertion — not 'avoid spicy food'
jokes.explanation: Michael's logical leap from 'opposite of eating' to rectal insertion is absurdist but internally consistent with his character. The rapid 'Nope. Nope. Nope. Nope.' reaction sells it. The joke is gross but the structure — he genuinely thinks this is the correct opposite — earns the punchline.

jokes.text: Pam to Jim: 'Sweetie, I love you, but you're really distracting me from my distractions.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to intervene and get Pam to go to the hospital; Pam is trying to maintain her distractions
jokes.punchline: Pam articulates the absurdity of the situation — she has become so committed to distraction that Jim's genuine concern is now the distraction
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect line. The paradox of 'distracting me from my distractions' is tight, funny, and character-true — Pam is the voice of reason who has ironically lost perspective. The warmth ('Sweetie, I love you, but...') makes it sweet and funny simultaneously. High economy, high quotability.

jokes.text: Talking head cut to Kelly and Creed (presumably) saying Jim is 'getting a little frazzled' and laughing at him
jokes.setup: Jim is visibly stressed and has used the word 'frazzled' which he admits he rarely uses
jokes.punchline: The cut to coworkers gleefully watching Jim crack under pressure is a classic mockumentary reaction shot
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary reaction beat — coworkers enjoying a colleague's stress. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head where he reanalyzes the contraction windows: '"Five to seven minutes." "Six minutes." Different, but not really. "Five to seven minutes."'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to rationalize why the seven-minute and six-minute readings aren't contradictory
jokes.punchline: He can't actually reconcile them and just repeats 'five to seven minutes' like a mantra, convincing no one including himself
jokes.explanation: Jim's desperate rationalization is a good straight-man in-over-his-head moment. The repetition of the phrase becomes the joke as his self-assurance clearly isn't working.

jokes.text: Dwight's contract: child shall be named from acceptable names including 'Ebenezer, Jebediah, Honus, Jedediah, Worf.' Angela: 'No Star Trek names.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is going through baby name provisions in the parenting contract
jokes.punchline: Among the archaic, farm-appropriate biblical names, Dwight has included Worf — a Klingon character from Star Trek — and Angela draws the line specifically there
jokes.explanation: This is a great joke. The list starts as period-appropriate Dwight (Ebenezer, Honus, Jedediah) and then 'Worf' appears — out of nowhere and perfectly. Angela's response 'No Star Trek names' is even better because it implies she might be okay with the others. The character integration is near-perfect: Dwight is rural, archaic, AND a nerd, and this joke synthesizes both.

jokes.text: Contract Section 5A: 'Child shall be male.' Dwight explains keeping the womb 'extremely warm for two days after sex, and then extremely cold for five months.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has included a provision that the child must be male
jokes.punchline: He has a specific (completely false) temperature-based method to control the child's sex involving extreme temperature swings over months
jokes.explanation: Dwight's folk-medicine approach to sex determination is perfect — the specificity of 'exactly two days warm, then five months cold' sounds like Schrute Farm wisdom handed down through generations. The confidence with which he presents clearly pseudoscientific information is core Dwight.

jokes.text: Jim tries to prevent Pam from getting in the car — Pam says she knows because 'You know me too well.'
jokes.setup: Jim approaches Pam, who is near the car
jokes.punchline: She reads his intentions perfectly and pre-empts him — the joke is the comfort and slight exasperation of two people who know each other completely
jokes.explanation: Sweet and slightly funny — more character moment than joke. The easy shorthand between Jim and Pam is warm but not especially comedic.

jokes.text: Jim asks 'Hey, did you change?' Pam: 'Oh, yeah. My water broke.'
jokes.setup: Jim notices Pam has changed clothes
jokes.punchline: She explains the reason with complete casualness — her water broke — as if this is a minor wardrobe explanation
jokes.explanation: An almost perfect joke. The setup is completely mundane (noticing a clothing change) and the payoff is massive (water breaking) delivered with total serenity. Pam's calm matter-of-fact delivery against Jim's horrified reaction is a comedy of contrasting registers. The economy is exceptional — 12 words total. This is exactly how the 8.0 anchor jokes are built.

jokes.text: Michael's response to Pam's water breaking: 'Too bad you didn't have sex, like, seven-and-a-half hours later. But you had to have the afternoon delight. I understand. Sometimes you have to go for it.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is scrambling because the water has broken and it's only 4:35 — they didn't make it to midnight
jokes.punchline: Michael turns the crisis into a meditation on the couple's sex timing and the concept of 'afternoon delight'
jokes.explanation: Michael's misplaced sympathy (for the insurance timing, not for Pam's labor) filtered through commentary on their sex life is characteristic. 'Afternoon delight' as the culprit is funny. Slightly too long to be as sharp as it could be.

jokes.text: Ultra feast menu revealed by Kevin: 'Hollywood theme. Ratatouille from Ratatouille, tandoori chicken from Born Into Brothels, and I tried to bake a cake like that District 9 prawn thing but I...' [trails off]
jokes.setup: Kevin has organized a ceremonial feast themed around movies
jokes.punchline: The film selections for a 'Hollywood feast' include a documentary about child laborers in India and a film about alien apartheid — Kevin's cultural literacy is completely random and wonderful
jokes.explanation: This is a terrific comedy beat. The 'Hollywood' theme immediately promises glamour, but Kevin's selections include Born Into Brothels and District 9 — prestige/art films that have nothing to do with Hollywood or festive eating. The specificity of 'tandoori chicken from Born Into Brothels' (what dish does this film inspire?) and the unfinished 'District 9 prawn thing' is brilliant. The prawn callback (prawns are the alien species in District 9) as a food item is a great double meaning. High originality.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's genuine moment: Jim confesses 'I'm scared. I'm real scared.' Pam: 'I'm scared, too.' Michael: 'I'm petrified.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are having a genuine vulnerable moment about fear of parenthood
jokes.punchline: Michael inserts himself into their private emotional exchange with his own fear, which is presumably about different or no specific thing
jokes.explanation: Michael's 'I'm petrified' landing at the end of Jim and Pam's intimate exchange is a classic Michael boundary-crossing beat — he cannot distinguish when he is and isn't part of a moment. The escalation from 'scared' to 'petrified' (more dramatic) is very Michael.

jokes.text: In the pre-hospital chaos, someone asks 'Should I bring a dictionary to the hospital?' Michael: 'The hospital will provide dictionaries. Bring the thesaurus.'
jokes.setup: The office is chaotically preparing for the hospital dash
jokes.punchline: A dictionary is a bizarre thing to consider bringing; Michael's distinction between hospital-provided dictionaries and personally owned thesauruses is surreal
jokes.explanation: Great absurdist exchange. The dictionary question is already absurd enough; Michael validating the premise but redirecting to the thesaurus — with the implicit belief that hospitals do in fact provide dictionaries — is a very good joke. Short, punchy, original.

jokes.text: Dwight appears with a tape measure, offering to check dilation. 'I didn't know we had a tape measure.' Jim: '"We" don't.'
jokes.setup: The office is scrambling to get Jim and Pam to the hospital; Dwight is trying to help
jokes.punchline: Dwight has a personal tape measure to perform an OB/GYN check on Pam; Jim's correction ('"We" don't') implies it's Dwight's own tape measure brought from home
jokes.explanation: Jim's correction with the quoted 'We' is a perfect straight-man line that implies everything without saying it. The image of Dwight bringing his own tape measure to measure cervical dilation is both horrifying and completely in character.

jokes.text: Stanley refuses to leave the bathroom during the hospital dash — multiple people have to physically deal with him as the chaos mounts
jokes.setup: Everyone is trying to rush Jim and Pam to the hospital
jokes.punchline: Stanley's bathroom visit is completely non-negotiable regardless of the emergency — he cannot be rushed
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Stanley's absolute refusal to be inconvenienced by anything is a reliable bit. Not especially innovative here but fits the chaos of the scene.

jokes.text: Driving to hospital, Michael gets distracted: 'This is where I saw that deer last week.' Dwight is escorting them on a motorcycle with a siren.
jokes.setup: Michael is driving Jim and Pam to the hospital in an emergency
jokes.punchline: He's narrating landmarks from his normal commute — while Dwight performs an unauthorized police escort — as if this is a leisure drive
jokes.explanation: Michael's touristic detachment during the emergency is character-perfect. 'This is where I saw that deer last week' as an emergency-drive detour is exactly how Michael operates. Dwight's motorcycle escort happening simultaneously adds to the chaos comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'I love escorting people. In fact, a few years back, I put an ad in the paper starting an escort service. Got a lot of responses. Mostly creeps. Made a few friends.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is explaining his love of escorting people on his motorcycle
jokes.punchline: He started an escort service via newspaper ad — the sexual service implication is immediately complicated by 'mostly creeps. Made a few friends.'
jokes.explanation: The word 'escort' does the double-meaning work, and 'Mostly creeps. Made a few friends.' is a perfect Dwight tag — he doesn't seem to have noticed the implication, and yet he's weirdly socialized through what sounds like a solicitation nightmare. The deadpan delivery of 'made a few friends' as the positive takeaway is very funny.

jokes.text: Michael reveals to Pam's mother in the car: 'She?' — the gender reveal — ruining the surprise for her.
jokes.setup: Jim, Pam, Michael, and Pam's mother are driving to the hospital; Michael is texting about them
jokes.punchline: Michael accidentally reveals the baby's gender to the grandmother who wanted to be surprised
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — Michael's texting causing collateral damage is a reliable bit. The timing (in the car, mid-emergency) makes it funnier. The grandmother's reaction sells it.

jokes.text: Dwight gets pulled over by a police officer for impersonating a police officer with his motorcycle siren escort
jokes.setup: Dwight has been providing an unauthorized police escort with lights/siren to Jim and Pam's hospital car
jokes.punchline: He gets pulled over — the logical consequence of pretending to be a police officer while escorting a car to the hospital
jokes.explanation: Earned payoff on Dwight's escalating helpfulness. The specificity of 'impersonating a police officer' as the charge is right, and the officer's 'Don't make this difficult, Dwight' implies a prior relationship — a great throwaway detail.

jokes.text: Pam insists they detour past the house to get her iPod with the 'birth song' on it — 'I don't want the first thing the baby hears to be the 8 Mile soundtrack.'
jokes.setup: They've forgotten the iPod with the baby's planned first music
jokes.punchline: Pam's specific fear is that her baby's inaugural sonic experience will be Eminem's 8 Mile rap battle music
jokes.explanation: Good joke — 8 Mile is a specific enough reference to be funny. The juxtaposition of Pam's presumably sweet birth song selection against Eminem's rap battle album is an effective comedic contrast. Pam's absolute conviction about this in the middle of active labor is the real joke.

jokes.text: Dwight's phone call to Angela to retrieve the iPod: 'We need it yesterday.' Angela: 'Then why didn't you ask me to do it yesterday? I kept IM-ing you how bored I was.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is calling Angela to pick up Pam's iPod urgently
jokes.punchline: Angela's response is perfect passive-aggressive logic — 'why didn't you ask me yesterday?' — deflecting the urgency with her own timeline complaint
jokes.explanation: Angela's literal reading of 'we need it yesterday' is perfect character work — she's both annoying and logically correct. The additional detail that she was IMing Dwight about being bored while he was dealing with the crisis is a great layer.

jokes.text: Pam tries to tell Dwight where the spare key is; Dwight: 'I don't need a key.' Pam persists; Dwight: 'Don't. Don't. Don't tell me.' As Pam keeps trying to tell him during contractions.
jokes.setup: Pam wants Dwight to know where the key is in case he needs it
jokes.punchline: Dwight's pride in being able to break into a house makes him repeatedly refuse information that would help him, even as Pam struggles through contractions to deliver it
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Pam desperately trying to deliver a helpful piece of information through contractions while Dwight keeps refusing out of pride is great cringe comedy. The visual of this argument happening mid-contraction makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Michael parks illegally right at the hospital entrance. Security: 'You can't park here.' Michael: 'I just did.'
jokes.setup: Michael is dropping off Jim and Pam at the hospital
jokes.punchline: 'I just did' — Michael acknowledging the completed action as its own argument, with zero follow-up plan
jokes.explanation: Three words that are perfect Michael Scott. 'I just did' is the ultimate non-argument delivered with complete confidence. Maximum economy — three words do everything. It's exactly the kind of line that becomes quotable because it's universally applicable.

jokes.text: Jim talking head from hospital: 'Pam's doing great. She's 10 inches dilated now. Sorry, meters... Centimeters.' 'And she's also fully effaced, which I don't know what that is.'
jokes.setup: Jim is giving a status update from the hospital
jokes.punchline: He confidently states the wrong unit ('10 inches'), corrects to the wrong unit again ('meters'), then finally lands on 'centimeters'; he then reports a medical fact he doesn't understand
jokes.explanation: Jim's two-stage unit correction and honest admission of not knowing what 'effaced' means is a great expectant-father bit. The structure of the self-correction making things worse before getting right is well-executed.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I was sent out for some ice chips because I might have passed out a little bit, but these are very refreshing...' [nurse interrupts] 'Daddy? She's ready to push.' Jim drops everything immediately.
jokes.setup: Jim was sent to get ice chips after a fainting incident he's downplaying
jokes.punchline: His casual understatement ('might have passed out a little bit') is immediately interrupted by urgent news — he dashes off mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: 'Might have passed out a little bit' is a great phrase — Jim's characteristic understatement applied to something embarrassing. The interruption before he can finish rationalizing it is good structure.

jokes.text: During the delivery, Dwight appears: 'No, don't push. Pull! Pull!' followed by 'Why don't you get some more ice chips?' to Jim, and then '...Gotta go wash my eyes. That kid's gonna have a lot of hair.'
jokes.setup: The delivery is happening; Dwight has somehow gained access to the delivery room
jokes.punchline: Dwight gives wrong obstetric advice ('Pull!'), gets Jim removed, then retreats to wash his eyes — implying what he witnessed was too intense even for him, but his parting observation is about the baby's hair
jokes.explanation: 'No, don't push. Pull! Pull!' is a great Dwight joke — he's either applying animal husbandry logic or is simply terribly wrong. 'Gotta go wash my eyes' implies the delivery overwhelmed even Dwight's iron constitution, and 'that kid's gonna have a lot of hair' as his only observation on witnessing birth is perfectly character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Michael has bought a framed newspaper from the day Baby Halpert was 'supposed' to be born. The baby took too long, so he now has to swap the newspaper. 'This frame set me back 55 bones.'
jokes.setup: Michael prepared a sentimental gift for the baby — a newspaper from her birth date
jokes.punchline: The baby took a different day to arrive, so his thoughtful gift is ruined and he's annoyed about the $55 frame
jokes.explanation: Michael's genuine thoughtfulness (he planned this nice gift) combined with his genuine annoyance at the baby for ruining it ('she decided to take her sweet time') is perfect Michael — caring and oblivious simultaneously. '55 bones' for a frame is a very Michael financial complaint.

jokes.text: Phyllis reveals she has an ice cream cake in the car. Michael: 'Oh, my God! Go! Go! Go! Are you insane?'
jokes.setup: The office staff are debating whether to stay or leave the hospital waiting area
jokes.punchline: The deciding factor for urgency is that Phyllis has a melting ice cream cake in a car — treated with the alarm of a genuine emergency
jokes.explanation: Michael's 'Are you insane?' — reserved for Phyllis's car-baking situation — is a good inversion of priority comedy. The ice cream cake crisis is treated more seriously than the labor.

jokes.text: Michael tries to check in with the delivery nurse: 'Sorry to be a bother, but if we could have an ETA when this is gonna...' Nurse: 'You're kind of losing them.'
jokes.setup: Michael is addressing the delivery nurse while she's attending to the birth
jokes.punchline: The nurse's 'You're kind of losing them' — referring to the crowd of waiting coworkers abandoning Michael, not any medical concern — is a great deadpan redirection
jokes.explanation: The misdirection in 'you're kind of losing them' — sounds medical, means his audience — is a good structural joke. Michael asking for an ETA on a labor/delivery is classic oblivious Michael.

jokes.text: Baby is born. Michael tries to light a cigar in the hospital. 'Sir. Sir, you can't smoke that in here.' Michael: 'Okay. Put it out. All right. Can't smoke anywhere these days.'
jokes.setup: The baby has just been born — a joyful moment
jokes.punchline: Michael's traditional cigar celebration is immediately shut down; his response is to complain about modern smoking restrictions as if this is a societal problem, not a hospital rule
jokes.explanation: Functional Michael joke — his indignation at 'can't smoke anywhere these days' in a maternity ward is characteristic obliviousness. Not the sharpest version of this Michael type but fits the moment.

jokes.text: Jim announces the baby name: 'Cecelia Marie Halpert.' Then starts with wrong stats: 'Eleven pounds, four...' Pam corrects: 'Seven pounds, two ounces, 18 inches.'
jokes.setup: Jim is announcing the baby's name and vital statistics to the waiting office
jokes.punchline: He almost announces an 11-pound birth weight before being corrected to a normal 7 pounds — Jim is still rattled
jokes.explanation: Jim's rattled state manifesting as an accidentally terrifying birth weight announcement is a small but good beat. 'Eleven pounds, four...' would be a genuinely alarming number.

jokes.text: Jim: 'You want to count her fingers and toes again?' Pam: 'No, let's let her rest. I'm sure there are still 12 of each.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are marveling at their new baby.
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'I'm sure there are still 12 of each' — implying they've been counting so obsessively that the number might change, or that 12 is the established count and she's confident it holds.
jokes.explanation: 'Still 12 of each' is an excellent line — it implies they've been counting repeatedly (anxious new parents) and that 12 is the established baseline. The deadpan delivery suggests Pam is so exhausted she's committed to an incorrect number rather than count again. Sweetly funny.

jokes.text: Pam's mother returns with coffee: 'It was an adventure and a half trying to find the cafeteria, but I have returned with the coffee.' Pam: 'Thank God. I haven't had caffeine in nine months.'
jokes.setup: The grandmother returns from a coffee quest
jokes.punchline: Pam's desperate relief at finally having caffeine after nine months of deprivation is both funny and deeply relatable
jokes.explanation: Observational joke about pregnancy deprivation. The grandmother's proud 'adventure and a half' for a cafeteria trip is a nice character touch. Pam's caffeine relief is universal and real.

jokes.text: Jim boasts he's 'a diapering master' after 'little else' in two months. 'There is nothing I cannot diaper. Go ahead. Try to think of something. I dare you.'
jokes.setup: Jim is confidently offering to diaper the baby
jokes.punchline: 'Try to think of something I cannot diaper. I dare you.' — Jim has become obsessively proud of a single parenting skill
jokes.explanation: Jim's swagger about diapering is a great new-dad joke — the challenge to name something he cannot diaper implies he's thought about this. It's endearing and slightly absurd. 'I dare you' as a parenting brag is very quotable.

jokes.text: Michael runs into Pam's mother Helene at the hospital — his ex-girlfriend. Awkward exchange. Michael: 'I worry about you.' Helene: 'I think it's time for me to go.' Michael: 'Love you.' Helene: 'Love you as a friend.'
jokes.setup: Michael Scott dated Pam's mother; they broke up; they now run into each other at his employee's baby delivery
jokes.punchline: 'Love you.' / 'Love you as a friend.' — Michael attempts a genuine goodbye and receives the classic friend-zone qualifier in a public family setting
jokes.explanation: The cringe of this reunion is effective — Michael dating Pam's mother was always an uncomfortable running story. 'Love you as a friend' is a perfect rejection phrase in this context, and the structure of the exchange (his 'I worry about you' as a romantic tell) is well-built.

jokes.text: Kevin shows up without pants to hold the baby. Jim makes him sanitize and then: 'Again. No pants.'
jokes.setup: Kevin arrives to see the baby; Jim has him sanitize
jokes.punchline: Kevin is not wearing pants — acknowledged after the sanitizer, as if the pants issue is a secondary concern to the hand sanitizing
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect visual gag structure. The sequence of (1) sanitize please → (2) comply → (3) ready? → (4) 'Again. No pants.' is impeccably timed. 'Again. No pants.' is two words that do maximum comedic work — the 'Again' implies this should go without saying. Jim's flat delivery (implied) makes it perfect. High economy score because the two-word punchline is all it needs.

jokes.text: Michael holds the baby and she seems to say 'Michael' — 'That's so weird. She was saying it just before you got here.'
jokes.setup: Michael holds Baby Cecelia and she appears to coo or say something that sounds like his name
jokes.punchline: Jim and Pam play along — 'She was saying it just before you got here' — which is an obvious lie to make Michael feel special, delivered perfectly deadpan
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny — Jim and Pam's gentle lie to make Michael feel included is character-true for all three of them. Michael's belief that a newborn is saying his name is characteristically self-centered but the Halperts indulging it shows their affection. Warm comedic beat.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: He was sent to find the iPod. 'I searched everywhere, but I didn't find it. What I did find was mold, and lots of it.' He then: 'read a book, had a bath, I got a good night's sleep, and I made plans to eradicate it. I also made plans to ask Jim where he bought his marvelous sheets.'
jokes.setup: Dwight was sent to Jim and Pam's house for the iPod during the hospital emergency
jokes.punchline: He didn't find the iPod but found mold, which led him to move IN for the night — reading, bathing, sleeping in their bed — and his only observation on their home is about the quality of the sheets
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the great Dwight bits. The escalation from 'failed to find iPod' → 'found mold' → 'moved into their house for the night' → 'rate the sheets' is perfectly structured. Each beat escalates the absurdity while remaining completely internally consistent with Dwight's self-justifying logic. 'Marvelous sheets' as his warm takeaway from squatting in colleagues' home during their delivery is exceptional. High character integration — only Dwight does this.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'There she sat. Her name was Pam. She was a receptionist. She was engaged to an animal.' / 'There sat Jim. He was a gawky, tall salesman.' / 'The odds of them getting together were insurmountainable.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a dramatic voiceover narration of Jim and Pam's love story
jokes.punchline: 'Insurmountainable' — Michael's portmanteau of 'insurmountable' and possibly 'mountainous,' delivered as if it's a real word in his dramatic narration
jokes.explanation: 'Insurmountainable' is a great Michael malapropism that sounds almost right — he's trying to be profound and lands on a made-up word. 'She was engaged to an animal' about Roy is also a good casual insult. The whole talking head parodies hardboiled narration while being completely Michael.

jokes.text: Michael: 'There sat Jim. He was a gawky, tall salesman.'
jokes.setup: Michael continues his romantic narrator account of Jim and Pam's story
jokes.punchline: 'Gawky' as the defining characteristic Michael leads with for Jim — not charming, not clever, gawky
jokes.explanation: Michael's choice of 'gawky' to describe Jim as a romantic lead is funny — he's not wrong, but it's an odd word to use in what's meant to be a romantic retelling. Consistent with Michael's narrator voice from the previous beat.

jokes.text: Michael's matchmaking offer to the office: 'I made a family. I got these two together and I made a family. This man has a gift.'
jokes.setup: Michael is crediting himself for Jim and Pam's relationship
jokes.punchline: He refers to himself in the third person ('This man has a gift') while taking undue credit for a relationship he had little to do with creating
jokes.explanation: Standard Michael grandiosity — third-person self-praise for an accomplishment he didn't achieve. Solid but not innovative within the Michael repertoire.

jokes.text: Stanley shuts down Michael's matchmaking: 'Why don't you find someone for yourself instead of meddling in our affairs?' Michael: 'Okay, show of hands. Who wants to live in a world where Stanley has two lovers and you don't have any?'
jokes.setup: Stanley challenges Michael's self-appointed matchmaker role
jokes.punchline: Michael reframes Stanley's polygamy (a known storyline) as the apocalyptic alternative to accepting his help — a wildly unfair but Michael-logical argument
jokes.explanation: Michael weaponizing Stanley's affair as a rhetorical device against Stanley's objection is clever Michael logic. 'Who wants to live in a world where Stanley has two lovers and you don't have any?' is a legitimately funny line that uses context knowledge effectively.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'I am never getting married. Like Clooney.' Michael offers to match Andy; Andy: 'Torn scrotum. Still on the mend, so...'
jokes.setup: Michael is canvassing the office for single people to matchmake
jokes.punchline: Andy declines on medical grounds — a torn scrotum — delivered with Andy's characteristic mix of pride and awkwardness ('still on the mend, so...')
jokes.explanation: 'Torn scrotum. Still on the mend, so...' is an excellent Andy line — he volunteers a graphic medical detail as a reasonable excuse for declining romantic involvement, with the 'so...' trailing off implying there's more to explain. Meredith's Clooney comparison is also good — she's claiming she's the female George Clooney, which is both delusional and slightly true.

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'Yes, I'm gonna ask out Erin. I'm just waiting for the stars to align. Literally. I have a small skylight in my bedroom, and I'd like for the moon to be visible.'
jokes.setup: Andy admits he wants to ask Erin out but is waiting for the right moment
jokes.punchline: His 'right moment' has an astronomical component — he has a specific celestial requirement involving his bedroom skylight and lunar visibility
jokes.explanation: This is a great Andy joke. The misdirection of 'literally' after 'stars align' sets up the expectation of a clarification; instead we get a very specific and absurd requirement. A skylight that needs to show the moon is both pretentious and impractical. The specificity ('a small skylight') makes it funnier. Andy's romantic delusion is perfectly concentrated in this image. One of the episode's better jokes.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's touching moment — 'Remember yesterday, when we were terrified of being parents? We were just kids. What did we know?' — played straight but arrives 19 hours after labor started
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are reflecting on how recently they were scared
jokes.punchline: 'Yesterday' was less than 24 hours ago and involved them refusing to go to the hospital, ultra feasts, and Dwight taking a bath in their house — the dramatic perspective-shift is earned but also very fast
jokes.explanation: Mostly a sweet moment, the comedy is in how recently 'yesterday' was and how much happened. Mild comedic effect — primarily emotional payoff.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam attempt to swaddle the baby — failing repeatedly. 'She's too strong. Careful, though. You don't want to break it.' Pam: 'She's not going to...' — Jim calls the nurse.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are trying to swaddle the baby for the first time
jokes.punchline: Despite Jim's diapering confidence, neither can swaddle — and Jim refers to the baby as 'it' suggesting he's reverted to uncertainty
jokes.explanation: Relatable new-parent comedy. 'She's too strong' and the immediate surrender to call the nurse are good beats. Not especially novel but lands in the moment.

jokes.text: Male lactation consultant Clarke arrives. Jim clearly uncomfortable: 'Do you want to try it, Jim?' Jim: 'Mmm-mmm. I think you're good. Doing a good job.'
jokes.setup: The male lactation consultant Clarke is demonstrating breastfeeding technique on Pam
jokes.punchline: Clarke offers Jim the chance to try the technique; Jim deflects with excessive compliments to escape involvement
jokes.explanation: Jim's discomfort with the male lactation consultant is a reliable cringe beat played well. 'I think you're good. Doing a good job.' as a response to the offer is exactly the Jim Halpert deflection voice — excessive affirmation as escape.

jokes.text: Clarke leaves; Pam struggles alone; Jim offers to try the technique he watched. Pam: 'Jim, please, please, please. I think it would be weird if you did it.' Jim: 'That makes sense. I'll just go get the other guy.'
jokes.setup: Jim volunteers to try Clarke's nipple technique on Pam
jokes.punchline: Pam finds it weird for her husband to do what a stranger just did, and Jim immediately agrees — then goes to find the stranger to do it again
jokes.explanation: The punchline ('I'll just go get the other guy') is excellent because it lands on the logical absurdity that a stranger doing it is preferable to a husband — and Jim accepts this instantly. The structure is tight: offer → rejection → immediate solution that highlights the irony. One of the episode's sharpest situational jokes.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Kevin to Erin as her 'new boyfriend': 'You will learn to love me.' Kevin is presented like a prize on a game show.
jokes.setup: Michael has decided to matchmake Erin
jokes.punchline: 'You will learn to love me' — Kevin presents himself with the confidence of a successful matchmaker's product while not being what anyone ordered
jokes.explanation: 'You will learn to love me' from Kevin is a great line — he's absorbed Michael's confidence and applied it to what is clearly a disastrous situation. The contrast between Kevin's certainty and Erin's visible discomfort makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Michael talking to Erin privately: 'Kevin has an enormous heart. Literally, he has an elephant heart. He had a transplant when he was 17.' Beat. 'No. Kevin doesn't have an elephant heart, but he is very sensitive.'
jokes.setup: Michael is advocating for Kevin as a romantic prospect for Erin
jokes.punchline: Michael invents a medically impossible (and horrifying) backstory for Kevin — an elephant heart transplant — then immediately retracts it, suggesting he knew it wasn't true but said it anyway
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional Michael joke. The pivot from 'enormous heart' (metaphor) to 'literally, he has an elephant heart. He had a transplant when he was 17.' is a perfect misdirection — Michael hears 'heart' and goes medically literal. The immediate self-correction without explanation ('No. Kevin doesn't have an elephant heart') is even funnier because we don't know if he believed it or was just trying it out. High across all categories.

jokes.text: Michael warns Erin about Kevin: 'I bet his heart is enlarged, though. I don't want anyone to die. Just don't let him sit on you.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to encourage Erin to lunch with Kevin
jokes.punchline: He disclaims all responsibility for Kevin's fictional cardiac condition and adds the practical warning not to let Kevin sit on her
jokes.explanation: 'Just don't let him sit on you' is a perfect Michael line — it's simultaneously fat-shaming (bad) and a sincere safety tip from someone who genuinely cares about Erin, delivered without any awareness of its cruelty. The 'I don't want anyone to die' is great because Michael has now created a real medical concern in his own mind about Kevin's fictional elephant heart.

jokes.text: Andy, hiding behind a hospital plant watching Erin and Kevin, explains to camera: In college he would hide behind plants in botany class to eavesdrop — but then he'd jump out and confront people saying 'You think all I do is hide behind plants and spy on people? Busted.'
jokes.setup: Andy explains why he's hiding behind a plant
jokes.punchline: His college eavesdropping strategy was to hide behind plants and then reveal himself accusatorially — a plan that only proves the thing he's denying
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly constructed Andy bit. The self-defeating logic of jumping out from behind plants to deny you hide behind plants is perfectly absurdist. 'You think all I do is hide behind plants and spy on people? Busted.' is a great line because the 'Busted' at the end is directed at himself as much as the observers. It's rich Andy character comedy — his complete unawareness that his actions contradict his words is pitch-perfect. One of the episode's best character jokes.

jokes.text: Dwight arrives at Jim and Pam's house to find mold — he's done new cabinets, moved the fridge to the backyard. Isabel: 'All I did was bring macaroni and cheese.' Dwight: 'Where's the fridge?' 'Oh, it's in the backyard. I'll take this.'
jokes.setup: Isabel arrives at Jim and Pam's house with macaroni and cheese to find Dwight has done extensive renovations
jokes.punchline: Dwight has moved the refrigerator to the backyard while addressing the mold — a completely unilateral home renovation decision in someone else's house
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Dwight has moved the fridge to the backyard while his colleagues are in the hospital is a great escalation of the Dwight-squatting-in-their-house bit. His matter-of-fact explanation and immediate takeover of Isabel's macaroni is peak Dwight territorial behavior. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight calls the woman (Angela) from the annex: 'Nothing left to do except dot the I's, the J's and the umlauts.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is finalizing the parenting contract with Angela (now revealed).
jokes.punchline: 'The J's and the umlauts' as things to dot — completely wrong, contractually absurd, delivered with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: 'The J's and the umlauts' is wonderfully specific Dwight pedantry. He knows you dot I's but has extended the rule incorrectly and added German diacritical marks. The Germanic detail fits Dwight's heritage. Very economical and specific.

jokes.text: Wrong baby: Isabel is holding a baby she's incorrectly identified as Cecelia Halpert. Pam: 'Wrong baby. This is not our baby!'
jokes.setup: Isabel has taken a baby from the nursery to show Pam
jokes.punchline: It's the wrong baby entirely — they've been cooing over someone else's child
jokes.explanation: The wrong-baby reveal is a great comedic moment — it's sudden, alarming, and funny in sequence. Pam's frantic 'This is not our baby!' has genuine panic that makes the comedy land hard. The extended beat where they were happily burping and cooing over a stranger's child amplifies the payoff.

jokes.text: Cut to the other baby's room: the other baby is sleeping perfectly quietly. 'She's not hungry.' Pam: bewildered.
jokes.setup: After the wrong-baby incident, the Halperts are told about the other baby's calm behavior
jokes.punchline: The accidentally-borrowed baby was sleeping peacefully and not hungry — everything the Halperts wish for Cecelia — played as a pointed comparison
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the wrong baby — the irony that the borrowed baby was easier than their own is a nice touch. Mild comedic beat but works as a scene tag.

jokes.text: The baby (actually theirs, now returned) 'is not hungry' — with the implication being the wrong baby was calm because it had just been fed in the nursery.
jokes.setup: After the wrong-baby incident, Pam has been trying to breastfeed. The baby keeps not latching.
jokes.punchline: The correct baby isn't hungry — possibly because the nursery gave it a bottle while they had the wrong baby. The bottle-confusion concern (nipple confusion) has been ironically realized.
jokes.explanation: A good structural callback — Pam's earlier fear about 'nipple confusion' from bottles is ironically vindicated, but through the wrong-baby mix-up rather than intentional bottle-feeding. Rewarding for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Nurse about checkout: 'That bottom part needs to go in the car.' Jim: 'Newsflash, the whole thing needs to go in the car.'
jokes.setup: The nurse is going over discharge instructions. Jim has the car seat.
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'Newsflash, the whole thing needs to go in the car' is a confident correction that reveals he understands the car seat less than the nurse does.
jokes.explanation: Jim's confident 'Newsflash' revealing his own ignorance is a good beat. The irony that his correction is wrong makes it funnier. New-parent cluelessness about car seats is relatable.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam are told checkout is at 3:00 — it's 2:35. Pam: 'Half hour.' Jim: 'Well, 25 minutes.' Then immediately asks the nurse: 'Can we get a late checkout?'
jokes.setup: The nurse tells them checkout is at 3:00; Jim and Pam absorb this
jokes.punchline: Jim immediately asks for a late checkout — framing the hospital as a hotel and himself as a difficult guest
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'Can we get a late checkout?' is a perfectly calibrated joke — it treats the hospital like a hotel, which is both the Halperts' entire plan from the beginning (getting the extra night) and an absurd thing to ask a nurse. The economy is great.

jokes.text: Isabel invites herself for a teeth cleaning from Dwight: 'Listen, I know that I'm an adult, but maybe I could come by sometime for a teeth cleaning? Just for fun.' Dwight: 'Well, adults are supposed to go to the dentist, too.' Isabel: 'Are they, now? How some people spend their money, right?'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Isabel are having a flirtatious moment amid the home renovation
jokes.punchline: Isabel frames adult dental care as a luxury hobby ('just for fun') and then marvels at how people waste money on it — suggesting she genuinely doesn't go to the dentist
jokes.explanation: Isabel's genuine confusion about adult dental care being a normal expense is a solid character joke. 'Are they, now?' to the statement that adults also go to the dentist is a great reveal of her attitude. Flirtatious framing adds a layer.

jokes.text: Andy sends Erin a fax asking her to dinner — the fax is sent to their own office fax machine. Andy stands waiting for the confirmation. Fax is busy; Erin says she'll keep trying.
jokes.setup: Andy decides to ask Erin out via fax
jokes.punchline: He faxes the same building — to a machine 10 feet away — and waits for a physical confirmation of the fax he sent
jokes.explanation: Andy asking Erin out by faxing the same office is wonderfully absurd and character-right — Andy's formality and need for ceremony overrides any practical consideration. The fax being busy adds a layer: their own machine is too busy to receive the fax from itself.

jokes.text: Andy demands Erin send the fax immediately or she's fired. Erin: 'You can't talk to me like that. I didn't do anything wrong.' Andy: 'I've been having a tough day.' Erin reads the fax aloud: 'Erin, will you have dinner with me? From, Andy.'
jokes.setup: Andy's ask-out fax isn't going through and he's panicking
jokes.punchline: He threatens to fire her over a romantic fax, then pivots to vulnerability ('I've been having a tough day'), then the fax content is read aloud making the absurdity complete
jokes.explanation: Andy's threat to fire Erin for failing to deliver his romantic fax is a great escalation of Andy's panic. 'I've been having a tough day' as the explanation-slash-apology is perfectly pathetic. The payoff of hearing the fax content read aloud removes all mystique from the romantic gesture.

jokes.text: Andy threatens to fire Erin for not sending his fax fast enough. Erin: 'You can't talk to me like that. I didn't do anything wrong.' Andy: 'I've been having a tough day.'
jokes.setup: Andy needs the fax sent urgently. Erin can't send it because the line is busy.
jokes.punchline: Andy threatens to fire Erin (from the receptionist desk he has no authority to fire her from). When confronted, his defense is 'I've been having a tough day' — an admission and apology in one.
jokes.explanation: 'I've been having a tough day' as the explanation for threatening to fire someone you're trying to date is a perfect Andy non-apology. It's self-aware but also self-pitying. Erin's 'You can't talk to me like that' standing her ground makes the dynamic work.

jokes.text: Erin reads the fax and reacts with genuine joy: 'Oh, my God. That's amazing!' Then immediately starts faxing it as instructed.
jokes.setup: The fax content has been revealed as Andy asking her to dinner
jokes.punchline: Erin's sincere delight at being asked out by fax — 'That's amazing!' — treats a mundane and slightly ludicrous method as a thrilling romantic gesture
jokes.explanation: Erin's guileless joy is a great character beat — she's not performing enthusiasm, she genuinely finds being faxed an amazing romantic gesture. This is consistent with Erin's characterization as someone who grew up in foster care and finds warmth in small gestures. Sweet and funny.

jokes.text: Pam has learned to breastfeed: 'There we go. Yeah. Oh, yeah! Like that. Oh. There we go. You got it.' Jim: 'Five tickets on the windshield.'
jokes.setup: Pam has finally gotten the baby to latch; they're celebrating quietly
jokes.punchline: Jim announces he got five parking tickets while Pam's breastfeeding breakthrough was happening — the mundane consequence of Michael's illegal parking
jokes.explanation: 'Five tickets on the windshield' as an offhand reveal during a tender moment is a perfect Jim timing joke. It's also a callback to Michael parking illegally at the hospital entrance. The juxtaposition of emotional milestone and parking ticket is well-executed.

jokes.text: Jim asks Pam if she used Clarke's move on the baby. Pam: 'I used a variation of your move.' Jim: 'Mmm-hmm.'
jokes.setup: The baby has finally latched using a technique
jokes.punchline: Pam credits 'a variation of your move' to Jim — who didn't do anything and was specifically excluded from Clarke's session
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Clarke situation — Pam gives Jim credit for something he had no part in, which he accepts with a satisfied 'Mmm-hmm.' Their domestic shorthand is sweet and funny. Jim's self-satisfied nod to a technique he never did is perfectly Jim.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about Erin and Kevin: 'There is no greater feeling than when two people who are perfect for each other overcome all obstacles and find true love. And that's what I thought that Erin and Kevin were going to find today.' Long pause. 'I think I'm going to be sick.'
jokes.setup: Michael narrates the outcome of his matchmaking with romantic gravity
jokes.punchline: After building to what sounds like a satisfying conclusion ('find true love'), Michael reveals it didn't work and his response is physical nausea
jokes.explanation: The structure here is nearly perfect: Michael builds with full romantic sincerity to 'find true love,' the pause lets the audience expect a payoff, and then 'I think I'm going to be sick' lands as a complete deflation — Michael's reaction to failure is visceral physical revulsion. The contrast between the grandiloquent setup and the blunt physical response is excellent. High across structure, character integration, and economy.

jokes.text: Final scene: Dwight presents a legal document to Angela at the office — the parenting contract. She signs. He signs. Beat. He looks up, she looks up. Both look away. Another beat. Dwight: 'All right. How would you like to celebrate?' Angela: 'Just pour yourself a cup of apple juice. I feel sick.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Angela have finished signing the parenting contract — they're officially agreeing to try to conceive
jokes.punchline: Angela's romantic celebration instruction is apple juice and she 'feels sick' — mirroring Michael's nausea exactly, but here it's about her own impending activity
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-closing joke. The beats of mutual avoidance, the awkward silence between two people who've just agreed to conceive, and then Angela's 'pour yourself a cup of apple juice' as a pre-coital instruction is perfectly bleak and funny. 'I feel sick' as the celebration is dark and character-true for Angela — she's pragmatic to the point of anti-romance. The visual of both of them looking away simultaneously is the whole Dwight/Angela relationship.

jokes.text: Bureaucratic bit: A nurse checks Jim and Pam's IDs to release the baby to them. 'Two forms of ID, please.' Then she does it again with the baby: 'And now you. Two forms of ID, please.'
jokes.setup: The hospital is processing the couple's discharge.
jokes.punchline: The nurse applies the same ID protocol to a newborn baby — asking the infant for two forms of ID.
jokes.explanation: Hospital bureaucracy applied to a newborn is a great bit. 'And now you.' directed at an infant asking for two forms of ID is absurdist gold — the nurse's monotone delivery implying she does this every time makes it funnier. Well-structured visual gag with excellent economy.

jokes.text: Dwight's elaborate parenting contract negotiation continues: 'Two forms of ID, please.' — referring to both Angela and the unborn child
jokes.setup: Dwight is in his formal contract meeting with Angela
jokes.punchline: Dwight requests 'two forms of ID' from Angela AND apparently from the (unconceived) child — treating the contract like a legal transaction requiring identification from all parties
jokes.explanation: Requesting ID from an unconceived child is a great absurdist extension of Dwight's legal-meeting approach to reproduction. 'Two forms of ID, please.' followed by a cut to 'And now you. Two forms of ID, please.' implies he asked both Angela and the baby. The paperwork extending to cover future beings is very Dwight.

jokes.text: Final tag: Dwight appears at Jim and Pam's door. 'I couldn't find your iPod.' Long pause. 'Give me a couple days. Be out of your hair.'
jokes.setup: The iPod subplot has been running all episode; Dwight was sent to retrieve it and instead renovated their house
jokes.punchline: He's still there. He didn't find it. He's asking for more time. At their house. After they've come home from the hospital with a newborn.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke and the payoff of the entire Dwight/house subplot. The escalation across the episode (sent for iPod → found mold → bathed/slept there → renovated → still there) culminates in 'Give me a couple days. Be out of your hair.' The casualness of 'be out of your hair' implies he is deeply in their hair. The scene of the new parents arriving home to find Dwight mid-renovation without their iPod is peak Office comedy. Structure score is near-perfect because this is the exact right ending beat for the subplot. One of the episode's top-tier moments.

jokes.text: Dwight calls: 'What? I couldn't find your iPod. Give me a couple days. Be out of your hair.'
jokes.setup: The whole episode, Dwight has been at Jim and Pam's house supposedly looking for the iPod, then renovating it.
jokes.punchline: Final revelation: he never found the iPod (the original task), has now been living there for two days, and needs 'a couple more days' before he'll leave. He's settled in.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the Dwight B-plot. 'Give me a couple days. Be out of your hair.' is extraordinary — he's treating Jim and Pam's house as a short-term rental he's been squatting in, and he needs a few more days. The implicit image of Dwight fully moved in, renovating, sleeping in their sheets, is the payoff of multiple callbacks. 'Be out of your hair' delivered with total nonchalance is the right level of casual trespass confidence. One of the top moments in the episode.

tmdb_overview: Sabre's CEO wants the Scranton branch to have one manager, and Michael voluntarily steps down and lets Jim become the boss when he finds out that salespeople make more money. However, he soon comes to regret the decision.
